title: June minutes explain why the RBA paused after three hikes while keeping further tightening open
summary: At the 15–16 June meeting all members voted to maintain the cash rate target at 4.35%. The minutes were published on 30 June. The judgement that distinguished this meeting from the preceding increases was that financial conditions were probably somewhat restrictive and were beginning to influence housing and borrowing. Inflation remained materially above target. The Board still expected a period of growth below potential to unwind excess demand, and explicitly retained the option to raise the rate again. It saw more value in observing how far three previous increases had travelled than in accelerating the adjustment before the evidence came in (Considerations for monetary policy and The decision).

Overseas energy and financial markets had reacted to progress towards a settlement between the United States and Iran. Oil fell, several countries’ bond yields declined, and short-term inflation compensation eased from earlier levels while remaining above its pre-conflict level. The oil futures curve was broadly back near the May baseline. Inventory drawdowns and additional production elsewhere had cushioned disruptions. Even an enduring agreement would require time to restore normal production and distribution, and refilling depleted stocks could sustain demand for oil during that recovery. The Board therefore distinguished a financial-market response to news from evidence that physical capacity and inventories had already recovered (Financial conditions and Economic conditions).

The global backdrop contained genuine divergences. The ECB and Norges Bank had raised rates. The Federal Reserve and Bank of England had held rather than delivering earlier expected cuts. Yields had recently risen in Japan and the US around stronger data, while falling in many other economies including Australia. Global equities benefited from earnings expectations, particularly in the US. Australian shares were broadly flat. Members considered weaker productivity, earlier rate increases, possible effects of tax changes on bank lending, and more limited direct participation of Australian listed firms in the AI boom. This was a comparison of market performance over several weeks, with multiple possible drivers, rather than an identified equity response to the June vote (Financial conditions).

March-quarter GDP had increased 2.5% from a year earlier. The headline matched expectations while its composition altered the interpretation. Household consumption had started to lose momentum before the conflict, public demand disappointed and private business investment was much stronger, especially in data centres. Some associated debt took the form of syndicated lending. Imported equipment meant that gross investment spending did not translate one-for-one into Australian domestic demand. Data centres also used Australian construction labour and other inputs, however, so strong projects could intensify skill shortages elsewhere. An economy with weaker household spending could still encounter sector-specific capacity constraints. The eventual productivity benefits of that investment were a separate question from the immediate strain on resources (Financial conditions and Economic conditions).

Weak economy-wide productivity made the wage data particularly important. The Wage Price Index was consistent with expectations and average earnings in the national accounts were slightly softer. Labour cost per unit of output nevertheless grew faster than its average over the inflation-targeting era because output per unit of labour was weak. The April unemployment and employment readings were softer than expected, while hours and underemployment were firmer and job advertisements broadly stable. Staff judged the labour market a little softer than anticipated but cautioned against drawing a large conclusion from one survey month. The forthcoming award wage increase was somewhat higher than the May assumption. Its effect beyond the lowest-paid workers would depend on bargaining conditions and inflation expectations (Economic conditions).

April underlying CPI remained consistent with the previous quarterly forecast. Market services, rents and durables largely followed expectations, groceries were softer and new dwelling prices were materially stronger as builders passed on some oil-related costs. International travel and a larger fuel-price decline contributed to a lower headline outcome than market economists had expected. A single inflation surprise thus contained little information about the direction of building costs. Short-term expectations had previously risen more than historical relationships with petrol and inflation implied. Most long-term measures remained consistent with target, with a sharp increase in union expectations in May the exception. Members did not infer from that one series that households and employers had generally abandoned belief in the target (Economic conditions).

Banks had passed the higher cash rate into lending and deposit rates. Scheduled mortgage payments had increased, though they remained slightly lower relative to income than when the same cash rate had applied before because incomes had meanwhile grown faster than credit. Housing demand weakened, with proposed investor tax changes and wider conditions also important. Business debt remained relatively strong. Estimates of the neutral rate put 4.35% near the top of the staff model range and above economists’ estimates, yet model uncertainty persisted. By the meeting, markets saw roughly an even chance of one further quarter-point increase by end-2026, down from roughly 40 basis points of further tightening priced immediately after the May decision. The June hold was widely expected (Financial conditions).

Consumer confidence was very weak but spending had not weakened materially in the latest readings. Historically the relationship tended to be weak and approximately contemporaneous. Investment intentions had edged higher despite poor business confidence. Together with possible easing of fuel disruption, these observations favoured assessing actual activity and margins rather than treating sentiment as a reliable forecast of recession. Risks remained in both directions. Lower productivity could constrain supply and prolong inflation. A larger housing-market downturn could weaken consumption more quickly. Energy costs could still reach future price and wage decisions even after the original fuel increase faded (Economic conditions and Considerations for monetary policy).

The minutes also record approval of a framework for additional instruments after feedback from the Governance Board. Any future advice to deploy a tool would need to identify the materiality of its effect on the RBA balance sheet. Further work on risk management and operational readiness would follow. No such instrument was activated at this meeting. For the purpose of reading the interest-rate decision, the policy news consisted of a pause at a level judged restrictive, the continued need for below-trend demand growth and the conditions under which another move might become necessary (Framework for additional monetary policy tools).

questions.question: Was the June slowdown concentrated in households or broad enough to release scarce resources?
questions.detail: Separate consumption, public demand and data-centre investment in real terms. Estimate the local input content of large projects and track hiring and capacity surveys in related trades. Compare with vacancies, hours and spending in consumer-facing sectors. A headline GDP number can conceal local shortages even while households reduce purchases and employment growth slows elsewhere.

questions.question: Did a lower oil futures curve actually reduce the probability of broader price increases?
questions.detail: Track fuel excise changes, imports, refined fuel costs and firms’ realised input prices alongside short-term inflation expectations. Follow products with different contract renewal lags, especially new housing compared with groceries. An early fall in petrol and headline CPI need not prevent earlier costs from reaching retail prices later. Look for changes in actual markups and wages as well as survey sentiment.

questions.question: How much household restraint came from rates, and how much from prospective property tax changes?
questions.detail: Compare established owner-occupier and investor markets around the respective rate and budget announcements, using loan contracts, deposit balances and borrower income. Match regions on prior demand and examine transaction volumes alongside prices. A simultaneous slowdown across both groups and mortgage-sensitive spending would support a rate effect. A larger change among affected investors may reveal an additional tax channel.
